method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty' (published 24 November 2025). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY ('distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License') (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12668195). Tables 1 and 2 (aetiologies; CHH genes) were stripped. An Italian review (Current clinical management of constitutional delay of growth and puberty, Ital J Pediatr 2022, PMC8944060, CC BY 4.0) was read and not used as S1: it is shorter and one oestrogen dose it gives ('5-10 μg/Kg per day') looks mis-stated.

claims.claim: **Delayed puberty in a boy: testes have not reached 4 mL (or 25 mm long), i.e. no move from Tanner G1 to G2, by age 14.** Pubic hair does not count, as it can come from adrenarche.
claims.source_text: In practice, this means the failure to change from Tanner genital stage G1 to stage G2, characterised by enlargement of the testicular volume to reach 4 mL or testicular length to reach 25 mm, by the age of 14 years (,). Pubic hair development is not considered in the definition since it may reflect the activation of adrenal sex steroid secretion, i.e., adrenarche ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Puberty that starts but fails to reach the adult stage within roughly 5 years, or stops, is also abnormal;** prolonged or arrested puberty usually reflects disease.
claims.source_text: The pubertal tempo may be affected, resulting in an abnormally low progression and the adult stage is not reached within roughly 5 years after the initial signs of puberty (); in some cases, pubertal maturation may come to a complete arrest. While pubertal delay may be transient, prolonged and arrested puberty usually reflect a morbid condition, as discussed below.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Self-limited (constitutional) delay is the commonest cause, 60%–80% of boys referred;** puberty usually starts by age 18.
claims.source_text: The most frequent cause of the absence of pubertal signs by the age of 14 years in boys is self-limited delayed puberty (SLDP), also called constitutional delay of puberty. In these individuals, which represent 60%-80% of boys seeking medical attention for absence of pubertal signs (,-), the onset of puberty usually occurs by the age of 18 years
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other causes:** functional central hypogonadism from chronic illness (10%–20%; e.g. malnutrition, coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, kidney or liver disease, inflammatory disease, diabetes), which resolves when the illness is controlled; permanent central hypogonadism (8%–10%); and primary hypogonadism (4%–5%, mostly anorchia).
claims.source_text: Another transient condition is functional central (or hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism, responsible for 10%-20% of the cases in males. It is associated with a wide variety of chronic or acute diseases, such as malnutrition, coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic kidney or liver disease, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and many others with chronic inflammation, Cushing syndrome, diabetes mellitus, etc. When the underlying disease is adequately managed, the function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is reestablished, and puberty progresses. … permanent central (or hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism (HH), which represents 8%-10% of the boys with delayed puberty, can be acquired or congenital. … This is rare in males (4%-5%) and is most often associated with anorchia (congenital or acquired)
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Favouring constitutional delay:** a parent with late puberty, gradual downward crossing of height centiles as peers enter puberty, delayed bone age and delayed adrenarche. These boys present slightly younger and are shorter and lighter than boys with hypogonadism.
claims.source_text: A family history of delayed puberty in parents, a gradual downward crossing of height centiles as compared to peers entering puberty, a delayed bone age and a delayed adrenarche are more characteristic of SLDP (). Patients with SLDP present at slightly younger age, and are shorter and lighter than patients with HH ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Red flags for congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH):** micropenis, cryptorchidism or small testes. Their absence does not exclude it: they were present in under 30% of boys with confirmed CHH gene variants.
claims.source_text: signs of deficient exposure to androgens in late fetal life and early infancy, such as micropenis and cryptorchidism, or of deficient exposure to FSH, leading to microorchidism, are considered "red flags" for the diagnosis of CHH (,). However, their absence should not rule out the diagnosis; indeed, they were present in less than 30% of males with bona fide gene variants of CHH ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look beyond the genitals:** about 40% of boys with CHH gene variants have other features, e.g. adrenal insufficiency, mirror movements (bimanual synkinesia), renal agenesis or dysplasia, cleft lip or palate, dental or hand/foot anomalies, and hearing loss. Reduced smell points to Kallmann syndrome.
claims.source_text: A recent systematic review () found associated manifestations in ~40% of patients with CHH carrying disease-causing gene variants. Particularly, adrenal insufficiency guided to variants in NR0B1, bimanual synkinesia or renal aplasia/dysplasia to defects in ANOS1, cleft lip and/or palate malformations and defects in dentition or hand/feet malformations were observed in association with variants in FGFR1, hearing defects guided to variants in SOX10 and, when associated with facial dysmorphism and cardiovascular malformations, to variants in CHD7 (Charge syndrome) … Early embryonic defects involving GnRH differentiation or migration together with defects in the olfactory tract result in CHH with hyposmia or anosmia, known as Kallmann syndrome.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **High gonadotropins with undetectable testosterone mean primary hypogonadism.** Broad screening tests for chronic illness are rarely abnormal without clinical clues. MRI finds CNS tumours or olfactory tract defects.
claims.source_text: Elevated gonadotropin levels and and undetectable testosterone in the hormonal assessment rapidly points to primary hypogonadism. Functional hypogonadism may be ruled out using broad screening tests (e.g., blood cell count, liver and kidney panels, blood chemistry, urinalysis, etc.); however, abnormal results are rarely found in the absence of clinical features or a history of a chronic illness (). Imaging, especially magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), has a role in detecting central nervous system tumours, or defects in the olfactory tract guiding to the diagnosis of Kallmann syndrome.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Basal or stimulated LH and testosterone do not reliably separate constitutional delay from CHH.** In boys aged 13 to under 18 with testes under 4 mL, FSH (IU/l) × inhibin B (ng/mL) below 92, or FSH × AMH (pmol/l) below 537, identifies CHH with sensitivity above 93% and specificity of 92% or more.
claims.source_text: The use of laboratory tests for the differential diagnosis between SLDP and CHH, essentially based on the measurement of LH and/or testosterone under basal and stimulated conditions, has not been completely satisfactory for many years (,). Conversely, recent studies focusing on FSH and Sertoli cell biomarkers, such as AMH and inhibin B, have provided significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy (-). The use of the product FSH (IU/l)×inhibin B (ng/mL) < 92 or FSH (IU/l)×AMH (pmol/l) < 537 show high sensitivity (>93%), specificity (≥92%) and positive predictive value (>92%) for CHH in male patients aged ≥ 13 and < 18 years presenting with a testicular volume < 4 mL and no other sign of pubertal onset (Figure 4) ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genetic testing by next-generation sequencing finds the causative variant in over 50% of deeply phenotyped boys** with suspected CHH.
claims.source_text: The efficacy of genetic testing has dramatically improved with the advent of high throughput techniques, such as next generation sequencing (NGS), allowing for massive parallel gene testing (,). The positive diagnostic yield of the underlying gene variant may exceed 50% in boys having undergone deep phenotyping (,)
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Boys with constitutional delay often present at 12–13 years worried about height and development. Reassurance and watchful waiting may be enough;** treat when the delay causes psychosocial stress, poor social interaction or depression.
claims.source_text: Boys with SLDP often present at the age of 12-13 years, with concerns about their relative short stature and lack of secondary sex characteristics as compared to peers. Reassurance of the patient and his parents and watchful waiting may be sufficient. However, when the condition causes psychosocial stress leading to negative social interactions and depression, pharmacological treatment may be necessary.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The authors indicate hormone treatment in constitutional delay by age 14,** to maximise height potential and peak bone mass and limit the psychosocial impact. In confirmed hypogonadism, do not delay treatment once bone age is 11 years or more.
claims.source_text: In patients with a confirmed diagnosis of HH, medical intervention should not be delayed, provided that bone age is 11 years or more. Similarly, in adolescents with SLDP hormone treatment should be indicated by the age of 14 years in order to maximise height potential and peak bone mass and minimise psychosocial impact ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Testosterone is the usual treatment. Typical regimen: testosterone enanthate or cypionate 50 mg IM every 4 weeks for 6 months, then increase by 50 mg every 6–12 months over 2 to 3 years to the adult dose of 200–250 mg every 4 weeks.**
claims.source_text: Testosterone is the most frequently used medication in boys with SLDP or HH (,), and the only one for males with anorchia or severe primary hypogonadism (,). Typical schemes start with testosterone enanthate or cypionate 50 mg IM every 4 weeks for 6 months, then increasing gradually by 50 mg every 6-12 months over 2 to 3 years until reaching the adult dose of 200-250 mg every 4 weeks.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If the testes enlarge on low-dose testosterone, spontaneous puberty has probably started and testosterone can be stopped;** keep monitoring until puberty completes, within 2–3 years.
claims.source_text: In patients showing testicular volume enlargement, especially during the initial stages of treatment with low doses, spontaneous onset of puberty is likely, and testosterone treatment can be discontinued. Nonetheless, monitoring is needed to ascertain that pubertal maturation is completed within 2-3 years.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Testosterone brings secondary sex characteristics, growth, bone density and better wellbeing,** but IM levels peak above the physiological range in the first week and fall low by the fourth week. Oral and transdermal forms have rarely been used to induce puberty.
claims.source_text: Other oral or transdermal testosterone formulations have been scarcely used to induce pubertal changes (). Androgen treatment results in the development of secondary sex characteristics and increased growth and bone mineral density, leading to an improved psychological well-being (,). There are, however, certain drawbacks in the pharmacokinetics, since serum testosterone peaks to supraphysiological levels in the first week and falls to low levels in the fourth week ()
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor full blood count, haematocrit, haemoglobin and liver function** (for polycythaemia and raised transaminases), plus bone age and height velocity.
claims.source_text: Side effects need to be monitored, especially by assessing total blood count, haematocrit, haemoglobin levels and liver function in order to identify polycythaemia or hypertransaminasaemia (). Bone age advancement may also need to be monitored along with height velocity.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Alternative in constitutional delay:** oral letrozole 2.5 mg/day for 6 months raised gonadotropins, grew the testes and sped up height growth.
claims.source_text: In individuals with SLDP, a 6-month treatment with oral letrozole 2.5 mg/day induced gonadotrophin secretion and testicular growth, together with accelerated height growth (,)
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Permanent central hypogonadism is treated differently:** a physiological approach uses pulsatile GnRH, or FSH first then LH or hCG, to grow the testes and support spermatogenesis. Whether this should replace testosterone in teenagers is unresolved.
claims.source_text: In patients with HH, replacement treatment should be centred on the administration of GnRH or FSH plus LH, if a physiology-based approach is applied. If gonadotrophins are used, the logical scheme should start with FSH in order to induce immature Sertoli cell proliferation and initial testis size enlargement, followed by the addition of LH or hCG (,) … Whether the latter should be preferred over testosterone therapy in teenagers with HH remains unsolved.
claims.locator: Rey RA, Grinspon RP, Castro S et al., Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 70(spe1), doi:10.20945/2359-4292-2025-0428, 'Clinical approach to the male with delayed puberty', published 24 November 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12668195/, retrieved 2026-09-23
